title.en: Writing formulae, properties of ionic and covalent compounds, molecular mass
A quick way to write formulae

text.en: A shopkeeper needs to know how many screws match how many nuts. A chemist needs to know how many atoms or ions of each kind make a compound. The criss-cross method gives this quickly, and the same ideas help us understand why salt conducts electricity in water but sugar does not.

keepEnglishTerms: ionic: high m.p.; covalent: low m.p.
ions must be free to move

text.en:
To write the formula of a covalent compound, write the symbols, write the valencies, and criss-cross the valencies as subscripts. Hydrogen (1) and chlorine (1) give HCl; hydrogen (1) and sulfur (2) give H2S; carbon (4) and chlorine (1) give CCl4. A subscript of 1 is not written.
For an ionic compound, write the cation first and then the anion, with the charges below the symbols, and criss-cross only the numbers. Calcium 2+ and chloride 1- give CaCl2; aluminium 3+ and oxide 2- give Al2O3.
Then divide the subscripts by any common factor. Magnesium 2+ and oxide 2- give Mg2O2, which is simplified to MgO. Calcium 2+ and carbonate 2- give CaCO3.
When two or more of the same polyatomic ion are needed, put it in brackets. Magnesium hydroxide is Mg(OH)2, aluminium hydroxide is Al(OH)3, and aluminium sulfate is Al2(SO4)3. Writing AlOH3 is wrong.
Now the properties. In Activity 9.4 you test camphor, sodium chloride, copper sulfate, sugar and naphthalene for solubility in water, kerosene and petrol, and for conduction of electricity. Use low-voltage batteries and keep petrol and kerosene away from flames.
Ionic compounds like sodium chloride and copper sulfate generally dissolve in water but not in kerosene or petrol. Covalent compounds like camphor and naphthalene are usually insoluble in water but dissolve in kerosene and petrol.
Ionic solids do not conduct because their ions are fixed in position. When dissolved in water the ions are free to move and carry current, so the bulb glows. Sugar dissolves in water, but it is covalent and gives no ions, so it does not conduct.
Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points because of strong attraction between ions, whereas covalent compounds usually have low ones.
Molecular mass of a covalent compound is the sum of the atomic masses of all its atoms. Water: H2O = 2 x 1 + 16 = 18 u. Carbon dioxide: 12 + 2 x 16 = 44 u.
Ionic compounds do not form molecules, so we use the formula unit, the simplest whole-number ratio of ions, and its formula unit mass. Sodium oxide Na2O = 2 x 23 + 16 = 62 u. Calcium nitrate Ca(NO3)2 = 40 + 2 x (14 + 48) = 164 u.

problem.en: Write the formula of aluminium sulfate and find its formula unit mass. (Al = 27 u, S = 32 u, O = 16 u)

text.en: Aluminium ion is Al3+ and sulfate ion is SO4 2-.

why.en: Write the cation first, then the anion.

text.en: Criss-cross the numbers 3 and 2: Al gets 2 and SO4 gets 3.
SO4 appears three times, so it goes in brackets: Al2(SO4)3.

why.en: Brackets are needed for more than one polyatomic ion.
Multiply each atomic mass by its number of atoms and add.

prompt.en: A solid compound does not conduct electricity but its water solution does. What kind of bond does it have, and why does it conduct only when dissolved?

requiredIdeas.en: In the solid the ions are fixed in position
In solution the ions are free to move and carry current

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all compounds that dissolve in water conduct
Thinking solid ionic compounds conduct because they contain charges

points.en: Formulae come from criss-crossing valencies or charges; divide by common factors and use brackets for repeated polyatomic ions.
Ionic compounds: soluble in water, conduct when dissolved or molten, high melting points. Covalent compounds: usually soluble in kerosene or petrol and low melting points.
Molecular mass is the sum of atomic masses in a molecule; formula unit mass is used for ionic compounds.
